set.body:
NEW BUG, found after the review closed while benchmarking the crossnobis path. Reproduced and characterised; not reported by any of the four reviewers.

REPRODUCTION. With 3 runs, the correct cross-pairing has C(3,2) = 3 edges:

  fit <- lm_relation_fit(responses, design, C, domain = domain)

  cross_partitions(fit$relation)   ->  3 edges     run1-run2, run1-run3, run2-run3   CORRECT
  cross_partitions(fit)            -> 10 edges     WRONG

THE MECHANISM. names(fit) is relation, error_models, capabilities, provenance, signature - FIVE
fields - and C(5,2) = 10. So cross_partitions() treats the relation_fit as if it were a list of
partitions and enumerates pairs over the object's OWN STRUCTURAL FIELDS. The left and right
endpoints of the resulting edges are the CONTENTS of those fields: nested lists containing the
whole source registry, extractor maps, whitener signatures and SHA-256 revisions.

CONSEQUENCES, in increasing order of seriousness:

1. It returns a STRUCTURALLY VALID effect_pairing. Class is c('effect_pairing','data.frame'),
   all the expected attributes are present - directed, self_pairs, independence, estimate - and
   the weights are populated. Nothing about the object announces that it is nonsense. There is
   no error and no warning at the point of the mistake.

2. PRINTING IT IS DESTRUCTIVE. Because the endpoints are entire nested field contents, printing
   the returned pairing emits roughly 80 KB of nested list dump. A user who does the ordinary
   thing - call the function and look at the result - gets their console flooded.

3. THE FAILURE IS DEFERRED AND MISATTRIBUTED. It does eventually error, downstream:
       Every pairing endpoint must identify a relation partition.
   That message is raised by plan_crossnobis, not by cross_partitions, so it points at the call
   the user made LAST rather than the call that was wrong. The result is not corrupted, which is
   why this is p1 rather than p0 - but the user is sent to debug the wrong function.

4. THE ASYMMETRY IS THE TRAP, and this is the part that makes it likely rather than exotic:

       plan_crossnobis(fit, ...)   ACCEPTS a fit          - documented, in the Rd example
       plan_geometry(fit, ...)     REJECTS a fit          - 'Relation fields are missing or
                                                            noncanonical'
       cross_partitions(fit)       SILENTLY MISBEHAVES

   Three functions in the same workflow, three different behaviours for the same argument. A user
   who has just written plan_crossnobis(fit, frame, ...) - straight from the ?plan_crossnobis
   example - has every reason to write cross_partitions(fit) alongside it. That is exactly the
   code I wrote when I hit this, and I had read every bead in this workstream first.

FIX: cross_partitions() should either accept a relation_fit and delegate to its relation - which
is what the user means, and matches plan_crossnobis - or refuse it with a message naming
fit$relation. Silently enumerating the object's fields is not a defensible third option.

While here, plan_geometry's refusal message is worth the same treatment: 'Relation fields are
missing or noncanonical' does not tell a user holding a fit that they want fit$relation. Same
class as the notes on bd-01KZY9B80RMYJD4QDAFS5ZBQSM.
set.title: cross_partitions() on a relation_fit silently pairs the object's own structural fields
